title: What time is it?
title_target: Τι ώρα είναι; — Tee oh-rah ee-neh;
goal: Tell the time, make plans, name the days, and learn exactly how Greek clock time lines up with English — and where it trips up speakers of other languages.
bekal: tell the time with και and παρά
name the days of the week
express a time span with από … μέχρι

dialogs.title: ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ — Making plans
dialogs.intro: Ana and Eleni plan their afternoon. Notice that clock numbers use the feminine form — τρεις, not τρία — because the word **η ώρα** is feminine.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: That late? When does the class start?
lines.literal: so — late? when — it-starts — the — lesson?

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: At a quarter to five. We have time.
lines.literal: at-the — five — minus — quarter. we-have — time.

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: At seven. Shall we go for coffee afterward?
lines.literal: at-the — seven. after — we-go — for — coffee?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Yes! But tomorrow I work from nine to three.
lines.literal: yes! but — tomorrow — I-work — from — the — nine — until — the — three.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: On Friday I'm free all day.
lines.literal: the — Friday — I-am — free (fem.) — whole — day.

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: Perfect. Eight in the evening, on the square.
lines.literal: perfect. at-the — eight — the — evening, in-the — square.

notes: ⚠️ **Good news: Greek counts the hour the way English does.** *Τρεις και μισή* literally "three and a half" means **3:30**, just like *half past three*. Greek names the hour that has **already passed**. Beware only if you also speak German or Dutch: their *halb vier* / *half vier* also means 3:30 but names the **next** hour — mixing the two systems is how people end up an hour early.

⚠️ **Clock numbers use the feminine form** because the word **η ώρα** is feminine: μί**α**, δύο, **τρεις**, **τέσσερις**, πέντε… So three o'clock is *τρεις*, not *τρία*. Only one, three, and four change; the rest stay the same.

**Και for past, παρά for to.** *Πέντε **και** δέκα* = 5:10. *Πέντε **παρά** δέκα* = 4:50. The turning point is the thirtieth minute: after half past, Greeks usually switch to παρά — just as English switches from "past" to "to".
**Στις + number = "at … o'clock".** *Στις οχτώ* — at eight. ⚠️ Except one o'clock, which takes the singular: **στη μία**. It's the only exception, and you'll hear it often.

**Days take the article, with no preposition.** *Την Παρασκευή* = on Friday. *Το Σάββατο* = on Saturday (neuter, hence το). *Τη Δευτέρα* = on Monday. There's no word for "on" — the article does the job by itself.

**Πάμε για καφέ;** literally "shall we go for coffee?" is the most typical invitation in Greece. Notice **καφέ** without an article: for a general activity, the noun stands bare. Likewise *πάμε για φαγητό*, *πάμε για μπάνιο*.
**Σύμφωνοι!** (*SEEM-foh-nee*, "agreed!") is plural because it covers both people. It's a direct cousin of English *symphony* — both mean "sounding together".

**Times of day always take the article**: **το** πρωί (morning), **το** μεσημέρι (midday), **το** απόγευμα (afternoon), **το** βράδυ (evening), **η** νύχτα (night). ⚠️ Μεσημέρι — roughly two to five in the afternoon — is a rest time still taken seriously in many neighborhoods. Phoning a Greek at three in the afternoon is like phoning at three in the morning.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: The pattern is always: **Είναι** + number + (και/παρά) + minutes. The word ώρα itself is almost never said.
after: **Asking:** *Τι ώρα είναι;* (what time is it now) and *Τι ώρα;* (what time is it happening). **Answering about plans:** *Στις …* For official timetables — trains, planes, cinemas — Greeks use the 24-hour clock: *Το τρένο φεύγει στις δεκαοχτώ και τριάντα.*
⚠️ **Ώρα means "hour" as a unit and "time" on the clock**, but not "watch" — that's **το ρολόι** (*roh-LOH-ee*).

grammars.title: Days, and how to attach time to a sentence
body: Greek day names are ordinal numbers, counted from Sunday as day one. Once you know that, four of the seven names come for free.
after: **Time spans:** *από τις εννιά **μέχρι** τις τρεις* — from nine to three. μέχρι is also used for places: *μέχρι την πλατεία* (as far as the square).

**Other time words:** σήμερα (today) · αύριο (tomorrow) · χθες (yesterday) · μεθαύριο (the day after tomorrow) · τώρα (now) · αργότερα (later) · νωρίς / αργά (early / late) · κάθε μέρα (every day) · το Σαββατοκύριακο (the weekend).

blocks.title: Greek clocks run slower than German ones
items: **A dinner invitation for nine means arriving at a quarter past nine to half past nine.** Turning up exactly on time at someone's home actually puts the host on the spot. For offices, doctors, and trains, punctuality applies in full.
**Dinner in Greece starts at nine in the evening**, and tavernas only fill up at ten. A restaurant that's full at seven is usually full of tourists.
**Small shops close during μεσημέρι** — roughly two to five — then reopen until nine in the evening. Big supermarkets and shops in the city center no longer follow this pattern.
⚠️ **Το Σαββατοκύριακο** literally means "Saturday-Sunday", so the Greek word for "weekend" names both days at once.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with στις, στη, or την.
items: Δουλεύω από ____ εννιά μέχρι τις τρεις.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
Translate into Greek. Watch the half hours.
items: The class starts at a quarter to five.
I work from nine to three.
Eight in the evening, on the square.
